text: Time to put this chapter together. The scenario: a user orders 2 licenses of the 'New Software License' catalog item from course 3, in one checkout, and you're designing its fulfillment from submission to close.

First, confirm the structural relationship from Lesson 15. One catalog item, quantity 2, in one checkout, creates one sc_request and exactly one sc_req_item — with its quantity field set to 2. That's one Requested Item to track, not two, which matters the moment your flow reads how many seats to provision.

Next, design the Open to Work in Progress transition. Provisioning a license isn't purely mechanical here — IT licensing has to acknowledge budget and seat availability first. So that transition is human-fulfilled: the item sits in Open, assigned to IT Licensing, until an agent acknowledges it and the flow moves it to Work in Progress.

From there, provisioning is mechanical: a REST step calls the external licensing system for 2 seats. Following Lesson 16's pattern, the flow does not close on a sent request — it waits for the response, checks that the returned license count actually matches the quantity requested, and only then sets the item to Closed Complete.

If the response comes back short — say, only one seat instead of two — the flow routes the item back to Work in Progress with a note describing exactly what the API returned, rather than closing a request that wasn't fully fulfilled. That one check is what keeps Closed Complete meaning what it says.

Open, acknowledged, provisioned, confirmed, closed — a state model that answers real questions instead of hiding a silent failure. That closes Request Management. Next, Chapter Five begins: Knowledge Bases & Articles.
